migration_summary: Data-only backfill migration (Django RunPython, atomic=False) reclassifying every 1:1 personal-message recipient into a direct-message-group recipient, across four large tables (zerver_message, zerver_archivedmessage, zerver_scheduledmessage, zerver_draft). Converted from the real Python orchestration to the representative core SQL statement it repeatedly issues per batch; the source is not a single DDL statement, it is a Python loop issuing this UPDATE (and matching INSERTs to create the new recipient group) once per 500-row batch pulled from a materialized temp table.
migration_sql: CREATE TEMP TABLE personal_recipients_to_process AS SELECT r.id, type_id FROM zerver_recipient r JOIN zerver_userprofile u ON u.id = r.type_id WHERE r.type = 1 AND (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM zerver_message WHERE recipient_id = r.id) OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM zerver_archivedmessage WHERE recipient_id = r.id) OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM zerver_scheduledmessage WHERE recipient_id = r.id) OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM zerver_draft WHERE recipient_id = r.id)) ORDER BY u.realm_id, r.id; UPDATE zerver_message SET recipient_id = $1 WHERE sender_id = $2 AND recipient_id = $3;
schema_summary: zerver_message (and three related tables) keyed by recipient_id, a foreign key that previously encoded '1:1 personal message' as a distinct recipient type from 'direct-message group', requiring every historical row to be re-pointed at a group recipient.

risk_flags.message: Work is proportional to total historical message volume across four tables, explicitly batched (BATCH_SIZE = 500) and run outside one large transaction (atomic = False) specifically to avoid a single long-held lock/transaction on a high-traffic messaging table.

risk_narrative: The migration is deliberately non-atomic (Django's atomic = False) and batches through a materialized temp table rather than running one large UPDATE, because zerver_message is a constantly-written, very large table in production Zulip installs — a single-transaction rewrite would hold locks and bloat WAL for the whole migration's duration. Idempotency for the group-lookup step is handled with an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING pattern so re-running a partially-completed migration (e.g. after a restart) does not create duplicate direct-message groups.
lessons_learned: For a backfill on a hot, high-volume table, prefer many small batched transactions over one large one, and make each batch's side effects idempotent (ON CONFLICT ... RETURNING) so a restart mid-migration is safe rather than corrupting. A migration framework that always wraps DDL/DML in one transaction removes this option; Django's per-migration 'atomic = False' is exactly the escape hatch this pattern needs.
surprise_notes: The bulk of the real cost here is invisible to a naive read of the migration file: it looks like 'a Python function', but at scale it is thousands of small transactions, each doing a per-sender INSERT/UPDATE — the actual database work is only visible by reading past the RunPython wrapper into the batching loop.

prediction_summary.risk_explanation: Duration scales with total historical personal-message volume across four tables on the specific installation; batched execution keeps per-transaction lock time low but total wall-clock time can still be very long on large deployments.

dimension_details.note: Real production migration from Zulip's Django migration set (zerver/migrations); migration_sql is a faithful excerpt of the real parameterized SQL the RunPython function issues per batch, not the literal single-file contents (source is Python, converted honestly rather than fabricated as raw SQL).
